prompt.context: Our client is Granite Investments, a financial services company in the US. It uses leading-edge technology in its business. A few years back, the client decided it did not want to invest more capital into IT systems and outsourced its hardware and support to a US-based company called Apolgee. The CEO of Granite Investments feels they are being overcharged for the outsourcing services and wonders what they should do. McKinsey has been hired to help them.
prompt.question: Why do you think the outsourcing costs are high? Help the client understand the situation and determine what actions they should take.

clarifying_info.q: What does the outsourcing agreement cover?
clarifying_info.a: Apolgee pays for all hardware and support required for Granite Investments.

clarifying_info.q: How many employees does Granite Investments have?
clarifying_info.a: 2,000 employees — every employee owns a PC.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost per PC?
What does each support person cost per year?
What is the general maintenance cost per PC?
What price does Granite Investments pay Apolgee per year?
What is the replacement policy for computers?
How many support staff are required?
clarifying_info.a: 2 support people are needed for every 200 computers.

clarifying_info.q: How many total transactions does the website handle per year?
What share of transactions are revenue-generating?
What is the average revenue per transaction?

framework: Understand why outsourcing costs are high: market structure (few vendors), client system complexity/specialization, high service level requirements, Apolgee's own cost structure, and transaction-volume inefficiencies
Quantify Apolgee's cost structure and calculate their margin to assess whether pricing is fair
Identify levers the client could use to reduce the price paid to Apolgee
Evaluate the specific proposal to upgrade service level from 99% to 99.9% for an additional $5M/year using incremental cost-benefit analysis
Synthesize findings into a recommendation for the CEO, including next steps such as competitive benchmarking

questions.prompt: Why do you think the outsourcing costs are high?
questions.guidance: A strong answer covers multiple buckets: (1) supply-side — few quality vendors so Apolgee commands a premium; (2) demand-side complexity — Granite's cutting-edge, specialized systems require premium support and skilled labor; (3) service-level premium — high SLA requirements raise cost; (4) Apolgee's own cost structure — possible lack of economies of scale; (5) transaction-volume driver — if pricing is per transaction, system complexity or process inefficiency could inflate volume.

questions.prompt: Calculate Apolgee's annual costs and profit margin given the data provided.
questions.guidance: The candidate must annualize PC replacement cost, calculate support headcount cost, and add maintenance. Margin = (Revenue - Cost) / Revenue. A margin of ~33% should be flagged as very high for the IT outsourcing industry.

math.setup: Annual cost has three components: (1) annualized PC replacement, (2) support staff salaries, (3) general maintenance. Revenue = $2.4M/year.
steps: PC replacement cost/year = Cost/PC × (Number of PCs ÷ Replacement cycle) = $1,200 × (2,000 ÷ 4) = $1,200 × 500 = $600,000
Support staff count = (2,000 computers ÷ 200) × 2 = 20 support people; Support cost/year = 20 × $60,000 = $1,200,000 ... wait — casebook uses: 60,000 × (2,000/200) = 60,000 × 10 = $600,000
math.answer: Apolgee's profit margin is approximately 33%, which is very high for the IT outsourcing industry.

questions.prompt: What can the client do to decrease the price paid to Apolgee?
questions.guidance: Strong answers cover levers on the demand/client side and the supply/vendor side: extend PC refresh cycle; reduce number of PCs in use; buy cheaper or lease hardware; reduce service level requirements; push Apolgee to hire lower-cost technicians; benchmark competitors and renegotiate or switch vendors (including non-US options).

questions.prompt: Apolgee has proposed increasing the website service level from 99% to 99.9% for an additional $5M/year. Should Granite Investments accept?
questions.guidance: Frame as incremental cost vs. incremental revenue. The client currently loses 1% of transactions; upgrading to 99.9% recovers 0.9 percentage points. Only 20% of transactions are revenue-generating. Compare incremental revenue gain to the $5M incremental cost. The deal is profitable if incremental revenue > $5M.

math.setup: At 100% uptime, total revenue-generating transaction value = 20% × 200M × $30. Currently 1% of all transactions are lost; with the upgrade only 0.1% are lost, so the client recovers 0.9% of transactions.
math.answer: The upgrade generates approximately $10.8M in incremental revenue against a $5M incremental cost, yielding a net benefit of ~$5.8M. Granite Investments should accept the proposal.

brainstorming.prompt: How can the client decrease the price it pays Apolgee for IT outsourcing?

categories.name: Reduce hardware costs
ideas: Extend PC replacement cycle from 4 years to 5 years
Negotiate a lease agreement with computer manufacturers
Reduce total number of PCs in use (e.g., hot-desking, virtualization)

categories.name: Reduce support costs
ideas: Lower the required service level (fewer support staff needed)
Push Apolgee to hire lower-cost technicians
Improve process efficiency to reduce support ticket volume

categories.name: Improve competitive dynamics
ideas: Conduct competitive benchmarking against other IT outsourcing vendors
Explore non-US vendors for potentially lower prices
Renegotiate contract terms using benchmark data
Switch vendors if contract allows and switching costs are manageable

recommendation: Accept Apolgee's proposal to upgrade website service level to 99.9%: the $5M incremental cost is outweighed by approximately $10.8M in recovered revenue, generating ~$5.8M in net profit
Apolgee's margin of ~33% is very high for the IT industry; immediately conduct competitive benchmarking to determine whether better pricing is available from other vendors
risks: Benchmark exercise may reveal switching costs that erode the savings from changing vendors
Website revenue estimates assume current transaction volume and pricing hold; any reduction would affect the incremental benefit calculation
Reducing service-level requirements or switching vendors could risk system reliability for a financial services firm dependent on cutting-edge technology
next_steps: Review existing contract with Apolgee to confirm break-clause terms (confirmed: Apolgee has agreed the contract can be broken if better prices are found)
Launch competitive benchmarking of US and non-US IT outsourcing vendors within the next few days
Model full switching costs (transition, re-training, downtime risk) before finalizing any vendor change
Renegotiate with Apolgee using benchmark data as leverage if switching costs are prohibitive
